newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's CDU presses ahead as German EMU fears rise.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's CDU presses ahead as German EMU fears rise.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) are stepping up their drive to win public support for Europe's single currency just as a new poll shows rising fears among Germans about giving up the deutschemark.

Only days before the European Union's Dublin summit debates the plan, the CDU gathered party officials and supporters in Bonn on Tuesday evening to reassure them the euro due to be launched in 1999 will be a safe and strong currency.

The guests got a strong pro-euro speech from Deutsche Bank chief economist Norbert Walter and glossy pamphlets packed with information to spread at the grass roots level in Germany's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia.

"We want to help break down prejudices against the single currency," CDU secretary general Peter Hintze said about the meeting, which is due to be copied across the country next year as the EU prepares for its economic and monetary union (EMU).
Those prejudices, though, seem to be on the rise.

A Stern magazine survey on Wednesday showed 61 percent of Germans polled now looked with fear to EMU while only 16 percent were hopeful about the euro. The level of EMU worries rose from 53 percent in October 1995 and 57 percent last April.
Only 26.4 percent of the 1,235 Germans polled supported EMU while 47.4 percent opposed it, the survey by the respected Allensbach group showed. Another 26.2 percent were undecided.
Expectations about Germany's economic performance with the new currency were also glum, with 45.9 percent expecting higher inflation and 35.2 percent sure that unemployment would go up.
But Allensbach said voters saw Kohl, probably EMU's main champion, as the best choice to assure stability in Europe.

Stern, a glossy weekly, played up the fear angle with a cover page showing a massive euro coin looming over the banking capital Frankfurt like the space stations that invade the United States in the Hollywood film "Independence Day."
Allensbach director Renate Koecher took a less dramatic view, saying pro-EU feeling always fell when economic problems loomed. "European integration as a goal is still supported," she told Reuters.
During the Bonn meeting, Hintze and Walter confronted German fears and prejudices with arguments German officials can be expected to repeat to worried voters in the coming months.
Hintze warned that growing competition from Asia meant the EU had to unite more or see its living standards slip.
"Nation-states, even ones as big and strong as Germany, are too small to deal with the challenges of the future," he said.
Walter chided worried Germans for overestimating their own economic virtures and overlooking the fact Bonn had won tighter controls on EMU than it imposes on its own regional states.

"This German smugness should be checked against the real facts in Europe," he said. "We do not realise that Europe has accepted Germany's stability programme far more than anybody ever expected, myself included."
There was an uneasy silence in the hall as he praised Italy's success against inflation, Ireland's roaring growth and Dutch pension reforms that are years ahead of Germany's.

As for the danger that weaker economies could undermine the euro's value if let into the EMU, Walter noted the mark had not suffered because of the perennial heavy deficits in small regional states like Saarland or Bremen.
"Why should it be any different with the euro?" he asked. "We have to accept that the mark cannot be the dominant currency in Europe in the long run."
